reason: The Court allowed the appeal because section 18 had to be used for adding parties and the plaintiff could not do so by amended plaint alone.
The Court expressly held that relief not prayed for could not be granted and applied that point to the attempted addition of parties.
The Court relied on section 839 not being available to override express Civil Procedure Code provisions and set aside the order on that basis.
The statement omits the material timing and partition context that the petitioners had acquired any rights only after judgment and therefore could not intervene.
The case held the opposite condition, namely that restitutio was unavailable because the petitioners were not parties and had no rights to restore.
The rule is materially incomplete because the Court tied the lis pendens point to the change from the 1951 Partition Act to the 1977 Partition Law.
The statement is only a vague reference to another case and omits the actual holding that the impugned preliminary-issue order was a final order.
The leave application failed because the Court could not assess a declaration of title without an intelligible land description and translated supporting documents.
The Court expressly held that it was not the Court's function to translate documents and treated the omission of translations as fatal.
The Court applied the settled rule that attorney negligence in failing to provide translations is negligence of the client.
The judgment made a fact-specific finding about no evidence of ouster among co-owners in a prescription plea, not the empty general rule stated.
The statement drops the material condition that the parties must be subject to Kandyan Law and the Court had found no evidence of that here.
This is a case-specific evidential finding about Salo Nona and Pemanisa rather than a usable legal rule.
The statement omits the essential qualification that although no party can demand a trial de novo, the judge retains discretion to order one.
The Court rejected the preliminary objections because the District Court order was palpably wrong and made without jurisdiction.
The statement omits the Court's material exception that revision may still be exercised where exceptional circumstances are shown.
The Court held that the District Court had no jurisdiction to set aside an interlocutory partition decree at the request of a non-party.
The Court used the need for a final decree after an interlocutory decree as a reason for holding the impugned order interlocutory.
The Court treated proper litis contestatio and adjudication on the merits as part of the test for finality of a judgment or order.
The judgment spoke of the final decree specifying separate lots and owelty, while the statement inaccurately generalizes this as a final order specifying shares.
The natural-justice holding was applied in the case, but the quoted administrative-body sentence is borrowed from another case and section 22(1) was not actually construed.
The Court held that a substituted heir was not entitled to a fresh opportunity where the original defendant had already been properly heard on the final plan.
The Court expressly treated section 121(2) as empowering it to require document lists not less than fifteen days before trial.
The statement is too vague and omits the controlling context of leave to produce an unlisted document under section 175(2) in the interests of justice.
The statement omits that the discretion concerned leave to produce an unlisted document and had to be exercised by reference to surprise, prejudice, truth, and justice.
